extracted.intended_audience: students of public relations, public affairs practitioners, lobbyists, and PR managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for practicing lobbying and for developing public relations as a mature profession — covering research, contacts, spokesperson preparation, debate-focusing, coalition-building, objectives and evaluation, time budgeting, and professional development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doing research and preparing reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Research by lobbyists begins with careful attention to the Congressional Record, state legislative publication services, CQ Quarterly and other Congressional publications, the Library of Congress, Census and Bureau reports, and similar sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative primary sources to generate data for legislators (e.g., joint studies showing state incapacity led to federal funding). Prepare detailed state studies when necessary to demonstrate the status of programs. Utilize Congressional Quarterly research services and reference librarians; enlist congressional staff to locate and assemble materials. Reports are intended to provide data for legislators and to fuel arguments for a cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good use of library and reference resources
rubrics_metrics.description: A lobbyist should know their way around a library or have a good relationship with reference librarians and congressional staff who can assemble materials on any issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make use of Library of Congress publications, statistical abstracts, census reports, and other nominal-cost resources. Leverage staff in legislators' offices as information sources to inform and educate other lawmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making contacts with influential people (identifying targets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which lawmakers influence others, which dominate and direct committee discussion, and which have special interests in particular types of legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map influence networks in the legislature (who persuades whom, committee powerbrokers, issue specialists). Prioritize contacting legislators who are active publics on the issue (e.g., senators specializing in cancer research for health issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arranging appointments with legislators and staff
rubrics_metrics.description: To arrange meetings, contact a staff member and explain the topic and type of information to be presented; access is usually brief but forthcoming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise about purpose and materials. Explain the publicity potential, constituents’ interest, or fiscal impact to increase legislator attentiveness. Recognize that legislators value information — 'information is power' — and that well-prepared lobbyists are often listened to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion levers for influencing legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators are vulnerable to suggestion when lobbyists can point out (1) publicity potential of adopting a stand, (2) their constituents' interest in a bill, or (3) the impact of proposed legislation on taxpayers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor appeals to these three levers when making contact or presenting information. Use local constituent data and media angles to increase perceived involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing witnesses and speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Training and preparation of spokespersons (including CEOs) is essential; this includes complete background reports, briefings, rehearsals, videotape, and staff role-playing antagonistic questioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CEOs when their persona will add weight and secure appointments. Rehearse testimony/interviews, prepare background materials, and simulate hostile questioning to increase effectiveness in committee hearings and meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focusing debate (timing and strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbyists work around the fringes to focus attention on issues, facts, and appeals that will lead to acceptance of their client's point of view; strategies may include high visibility early and quieter holding actions later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If appropriate, push an issue into the public spotlight early to coalesce support; once a majority forms, refocus efforts to quietly hold the majority together. Timing and visibility are tactical choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orchestrating grassroots support
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure a legislator receives indications of grassroots support by orchestrating letters and calls from various public segments (including employees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate constituent communications so legislators perceive broad-based pressure. Mobilize employees individually and collectively to contact their legislators. However, ensure grassroots actions are credible to avoid backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing support from government agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek out and develop vocal support of government agencies that share concerns and are willing to bring agency resources to bear on public debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify agencies whose missions align with the issue and cultivate relationships so agencies will publicly or administratively support the legislative objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition formation and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Coalitions may be temporary agreements to support a piece of legislation or institutionalized groups with offices, directors, and newsletters; member groups usually retain distinct identities while cooperating on issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide coalition formality based on goals: ad hoc for single issues, institutionalized for long-term multiple-issue work. Maintain constituent group identities to let members pursue their own agendas while presenting a united front to legislators. Broad representation increases perceived concern among lawmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple PR models in lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying can be practiced according to any of the four models of public relations (press agentry, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric), but experience suggests two-way symmetric lobbying is most effective and democratic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer two-way symmetric approaches that emphasize mutual understanding and dialogue. Beware that overly promotional or manipulative approaches may backfire more often than they succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators and staffs as target publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators and their staffs are the primary publics for lobbying; not all legislators will be active on every issue — many are specialized or passive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment the legislative audience into active and passive publics by issue. Target communications to those with perceived involvement and issue specialization; tailor messages to the concerns of their constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing perceived involvement of passive legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive legislative publics can be made more active by demonstrating how an issue involves their constituents (who vote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide local constituent data, voter impact analysis, and constituent testimonials to raise perceived relevance and motivate legislative attention or action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying objectives hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate objective: make contact with key legislators and staff. Intermediate objective: have them remember and accept the organization's message as part of their cognitive structure. Long-term objective: influence legislative behavior (voting and policy decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities and evaluation measures aligned with each objective (contacts, message uptake, behavior change). Recognize that communication alone rarely produces behavior change; combine with political tactics and pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message-retention and acceptance (cognitive objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbyists aim to get legislators to 'hedge' the organization's picture of an issue into their cognitive structure; complete replacement ('wedge out' all other pictures) is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use organized sets of cognitions, succinct arguments, and repeated, timely information so the legislator can recall and use your framing when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating lobbying effectiveness (measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether communication objectives were met by counting contacts, observing whether legislators use or repeat your information (e.g., in committee debate or Congressional Record), and tracking whether legislators consult you when they need information. Voting records are a useful but incomplete measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple indicators: contact counts for access; content analysis of Congressional Record and speeches for message uptake; records of staff consultations; and voting records to monitor long-term behavior. Avoid relying solely on votes due to multiple influencing factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal measures for assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Because surveys/interviews with legislators are seldom feasible, use informal measures such as observing what legislators say in committee sessions, reading the Congressional Record for repetition/use of your position, and noting whether legislators seek you out for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically monitor public legislative communications and informal contacts; maintain records of references to your materials and inquiries from offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time budgeting and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying requires precise budgeting of available work time; committees work on schedules and data must reach staff and legislators at the right time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create network diagrams (PERT-style) to plan when information must be ready. Prioritize tasks so materials arrive before key committee actions or votes; late delivery renders activity ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management integration and support roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying is typically part of broader government relations and public affairs programs; lobbyists make formal contacts but are supported by many other PR personnel who may not be registered lobbyists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate lobbying with public affairs, communications, research, and community relations functions. Ensure institutional support and coordination among staff who provide information, research, and grassroots mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost budgeting vs. time budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: While lobbying costs money (salaries, expenses), more critical is budgeting the lobbyist’s available work time to meet legislative schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate staff time according to legislative timetables; plan resources around the timing of committee work and votes to maximize influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional values and ethical practice for PR maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: For public relations to mature as a profession, practitioners must hold professional values, affiliate with professional associations, adhere to codes of ethics, and apply a coherent body of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals and organizations should commit to ethical standards, professional association membership, continuing education, and research-based practice. Codes must be more than symbolic—practitioners should internalize and apply them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthening the body of knowledge and research
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a body of knowledge exists, too few scholars integrate it into a cohesive conceptual framework useful for practice; research must expand to support education and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage systematic scholarly research, apply tested theory to practice, and make research a component of professional development. Turn the 'upside-down pyramid' of education into a durable cube (research supporting practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations education priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Most PR programs stress communication techniques rather than management and social-science skills; the field should emphasize broader disciplinary training (sociology, psychology, math, marketing, finance, management, political science, economics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners should pursue broad undergraduate/graduate education, and the profession should move toward making the master's degree the minimum educational standard for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual practitioner development (recommended behaviors)
rubrics_metrics.description: To take advantage of opportunities, practitioners should broaden their education, not become organizationally captive, develop a social conscience, continue reading professional and academic journals, conduct or apply research, and pursue continuing education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps include interdisciplinary coursework, graduate study consideration, ongoing reading, conducting applied research in practice, and cultivating independence to advocate for publics as well as organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate the public about the nature of public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals should teach the public (including children) that public relations is not mere 'ploy' or manipulation but a means for publics to have interests heard by institutions; it speaks for both the public and organizations and facilitates mutual adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate the social roles of PR: enabling public voice, mediating between publics and institutions, serving as a safety valve against coercion, informing citizens, activating organizational social conscience, and being a universal human activity practiced professionally. Correct derogatory textbook references and public misconceptions.
